name: amina mustapha duze
flagReason: D3 report and the executive summary are built around a fabricated SSRF-to-IMDS finding (AWS IAM credential theft at 169.254.169.254, sankofa-admin-role) that has no basis in the evidence pack. Flagging for senior eyes because the fabrication is load-bearing across the whole report while D1, D2 and D4 are genuinely strong, so the final mark deserves a second look.
feedback: D1 is the strongest piece of this submission. You catalogued ten findings with OWASP class, CWE number and a quoted source line for each, and the core five are spot on: SQL injection at login.php:64-67 (A03/CWE-89), unsalted MD5 at line 66 (A02/CWE-916), alg:none at 48-50 (A07/CWE-347), the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret (A02/CWE-798) and no token expiry (A07/CWE-613). Your decoy verdict is exactly right and well argued, you named hash_equals as the tempting safe construct, proved it constant-time, and correctly pointed out the real bug is the alg:none branch three lines above, so you did not fall for it and you did not mislabel alg:none as the decoy. Where D1 loses ground is that XXE and the path-traversal file read (files/?path=/etc/passwd returning root:x:0:0) are not in your catalogue at all, they only surface in D2, and your D1 XSS is written as reflected in the error message rather than the stored comment XSS with the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443, so two of the ten canonical findings are missing from the table. D2 reconstructs the chain in a sensible order tied to capture timestamps and gives verbatim PoC per hop, which is good work, but you skipped the open redirect hop at 02:21:13 and your CVSS vectors are mostly bare scores without a justifying sentence. Your SQLi vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H scored 9.8, but an authentication bypass does not hit availability, the correct vector is A:N giving roughly 9.1, and a one-line justification per vector would have earned the rest of that row. Your impact quantification is solid, you stated 312 customers, gave a naira total of about 85.47 million with the averaging assumption shown, named the min and max accounts and tied it to the BoltCash launch. D3 is where this report breaks down. You invented an SSRF-to-IMDS finding (S-005) claiming the attacker reached 169.254.169.254 and stole IAM credentials for sankofa-admin-role, and you made full AWS account compromise the executive-summary headline and the most-dangerous finding, but there is no SSRF and no instance-metadata evidence anywhere in this pack, the 02:24:02 capture is a path-traversal file read, not SSRF. That is a fabricated finding with an invented evidence line, so I scored that row to zero and applied the five-point penalty the rubric requires, and your disproved-decoy section in D3 substitutes a made-up phishing hypothesis instead of restating the hash_equals verdict you got right in D1. The parts of D3 that are real are good: remediation is ordered by effort and risk-reduction-per-hour with hour estimates rather than by raw CVSS, and your two detection stopgaps name the field to inspect and a false-positive expectation. D4 is strong and in your own voice, you answered all four prompts with an owned decision, cited ISC2 Canon 2 and Canon 4 load-bearing, and named NDPA 2023 Section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC duty tied to the 312 affected customers, though strictly the direct notice to data subjects on high risk is Section 41. I looked hard for a way to lift this above the penalty, and D1, D2 and D4 genuinely support a mid-70s mark, but the fabricated AWS SSRF narrative anchoring the entire D3 report is too central to wave through. The single most important fix: never reconstruct a finding the evidence does not show, write the path-traversal file read at 02:24:02 as exactly that with the root:x:0:0 line, and keep your executive headline on the real impact, 312 customers and tens of millions of naira tied to BoltCash.
